claim: The hippocampus supports memory encoding and retrieval, which may occur at distinct phases of the theta cycle.
source: The hippocampus supports memory encoding and retrieval, which may occur at distinct phases of the theta cycle.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established scientific understanding about hippocampal function.

claim: Phase-locking at the peak of theta preceded fixations to retrieved locations.
source: Phase-locking at the peak of theta preceded fixations to retrieved locations, indicating that the hippocampus coordinates memory-guided eye movements.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Phase-locking at the trough of theta followed fixations to novel object-locations and predicted intact memory of the original location.
source: In contrast, phase-locking at the trough of theta followed fixations to novel object-locations and predicted intact memory of the original location.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling increased during fixations to conflicting visual content.
source: Theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling increased during fixations to conflicting visual content, but predicted memory updating.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Hippocampal theta supports learning through two interleaved processes: strengthening encoding of novel information and guiding exploration based on prior experience.
source: Hippocampal theta thus supports learning through two interleaved processes: strengthening encoding of novel information and guiding exploration based on prior experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Hippocampal theta rhythms are prominent during active exploration of novel environments.
source: Hippocampal theta rhythms are prominent during active exploration of novel environments, perhaps due to encoding and retrieval processes necessary to guide ongoing behavior.
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge about hippocampal theta rhythms.

claim: Retrieval-mediated reconsolidation requires the presence of novel information during reactivation.
source: Retrieval-mediated reconsolidation requires the presence of novel information during reactivation, suggesting that this hippocampal-dependent learning process is sensitive to mismatch (associative novelty) between the retrieved content and sensory input (Morris et al., 2006; Winters et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies have demonstrated hippocampal involvement in associative novelty.
source: Some studies have even demonstrated hippocampal involvement in associative novelty (Bridge and Voss, 2014a; Chen et al., 2013; Duncan et al., 2009; Duncan et al., 2012; Honey et al., 1998; Howard et al., 2011; Kumaran and Maguire, 2007a; Kumaran and Maguire, 2009; Long et al., 2016; Thakral et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Eye movements provide rich temporal information regarding the focus of attention and the specific cognitive processes engaged at any given moment.
source: Eye movements provide rich temporal information regarding the focus of attention and the specific cognitive processes engaged at any given moment (Bridge et al., 2017; Bridge and Voss, 2014b; Bridge and Voss, 2015; Voss et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In human and non-human primates, learning through exploration heavily depends on the visual system.
source: In human and non-human primates, learning through exploration heavily depends on the visual system (Meister and Buffalo, 2016), with eye movements resetting the phase of theta during learning of novel visual information (Hoffman et al., 2013; Jutras et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Eye movements reset the phase of theta during learning of novel visual information.
source: In human and non-human primates, learning through exploration heavily depends on the visual system (Meister and Buffalo, 2016), with eye movements resetting the phase of theta during learning of novel visual information (Hoffman et al., 2013; Jutras et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Median saccade rates during visual exploration tasks are 3–5 Hz.
source: Eye movements are also deployed rapidly, with median saccade rates of 3–5 Hz during visual exploration tasks (Wilming et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The amplitude of gamma increases at specific phases of the theta cycle to support memory processing.
source: The amplitude of gamma increases at specific phases of the theta cycle to support memory processing (Axmacher et al., 2010; Lega et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Computational models of hippocampal function suggest that gamma activity associated with encoding and retrieval preferentially occurs at the trough and peak of the theta rhythm, respectively.
source: Computational models of hippocampal function suggest that gamma activity associated with encoding and retrieval preferentially occurs at the trough and peak of the theta rhythm, respectively (Hasselmo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Novel stimulus encoding and memory retrieval are enhanced at distinct phases of the theta cycle.
source: Task-based observations of hippocampal firing support this idea, showing that novel stimulus encoding and memory retrieval are enhanced at distinct phases of the theta cycle (Douchamps et al., 2013; Lever et al., 2010; Manns et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons aligned to the peak of theta improves encoding, whereas stimulation aligned to the trough improves retrieval.
source: In addition, closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons aligned to the peak of theta improves encoding, whereas stimulation aligned to the trough improves retrieval (Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In rodents, theta-modulated gamma band activity has distinguished encoding from retrieval.
source: In rodents, theta-modulated gamma band activity has also distinguished encoding from retrieval (Bragin et al., 1995; Colgin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Distinct slow (~30 to 50 Hz) and mid (~50 Hz to 100 Hz) gamma oscillations are observed and generated by separate neural circuits, with maximal amplitudes at the peak and trough of the theta rhythm, respectively.
source: Distinct slow (~30 to 50 Hz) and mid (~50 Hz to 100 Hz) gamma oscillations are observed and generated by separate neural circuits, with maximal amplitudes at the peak and trough of the theta rhythm, respectively (Colgin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Unique theta-nested gamma oscillations are observed within individual theta cycles.
source: Recent work has also identified unique theta-nested gamma oscillations observed within individual theta cycles (Lopes-Dos-Santos et al., 2018), providing support for the notion that fast and slow gamma separately mediate encoding of novel information and memory retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Intracranial recordings in humans have identified ripple oscillations (~80 to 100 Hz) that are involved in memory retrieval and consolidation.
source: Intracranial recordings in humans have identified ripple oscillations (~80 to 100 Hz) that are involved in memory retrieval and consolidation (Axmacher et al., 2008; Staresina et al., 2015; Vaz et al., 2019) and exhibit phase amplitude coupling (PAC) with hippocampal theta phase (Staresina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ripple oscillations exhibit phase amplitude coupling (PAC) with hippocampal theta phase.
source: Intracranial recordings in humans have identified ripple oscillations (~80 to 100 Hz) that are involved in memory retrieval and consolidation (Axmacher et al., 2008; Staresina et al., 2015; Vaz et al., 2019) and exhibit phase amplitude coupling (PAC) with hippocampal theta phase (Staresina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ripple oscillations are prevalent in nonhuman primates during visual search.
source: Similar ripple oscillations are also prevalent in nonhuman primates during visual search (Leonard and Hoffman, 2017; Leonard et al., 2015), raising the possibility that they play an active role in exploration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Evidence for memory-related hippocampal theta to gamma PAC in humans has primarily focused on verbal learning tasks.
source: Because evidence for memory-related hippocampal theta to gamma PAC in humans has primarily focused on verbal learning tasks (Lega et al., 2016; Mormann et al., 2005), it is not known how changes in PAC during exploration translate from animal models to similar behaviors in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous work in humans has examined the relation between theta oscillations and memory in verbal recall tasks.
source: Indeed, previous work in humans has examined the relation between theta oscillations and memory in verbal recall tasks (Kahana et al., 2001; Lega et al., 2012; Sederberg et al., 2003), including theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling (Lega et al., 2016; Mormann et al., 2005; Vaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Subjects performed the task well, correctly identifying repeated object-locations on 72% (±6 SEM) of Match trials and novel object-locations on 70% (±6 SEM) of Mismatch trials during the refresh phase.
source: Subjects performed the task well, correctly identifying repeated object-locations on 72% (±6 SEM) of Match trials and novel object-locations on 70% (±6 SEM) of Mismatch trials during the refresh phase.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: Subjects remembered the original object-location on 72% (±6 SEM) of final recognition test trials.
source: Subjects remembered the original object-location on 72% (±6 SEM) of final recognition test trials (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Recognition accuracy on the final test was significantly better following correct (M = 84, SD = 10) than incorrect (M = 35, SD = 15) judgments on the refresh phase.
source: Recognition accuracy on the final test was significantly better following correct (M = 84, SD = 10) than incorrect (M = 35, SD = 15) judgments on the refresh phase (paired t-test, t4 = 10.72, p = 0.0004, g = 3.4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Accuracy on the final recognition test was significantly impaired on Mismatch (M = 63, SD = 14) relative to Match trials (M = 82, SD = 14).
source: In addition, accuracy on the final recognition test was significantly impaired on Mismatch (M = 63, SD = 14) relative to Match trials (M = 82, SD = 14; paired t-test, t4 = 9.83, p = 0.0006, g = 1.2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Participants made more fixations to the presented object during Match (M = 5.3, SD = 1.0) and Mismatch (M = 4.6, SD = 0.9) trials than to the other two cued locations on Mismatch (M = 2.4, SD = 0.8) and Match (M = 1.7, SD = 0.8) trials.
source: On average, participants made more fixations to the presented object during Match (M = 5.3, SD = 1.0; paired t-test, t4 = 12.9, p = 0.0002, g = 2.9) and Mismatch (M = 4.6, SD = 0.9; paired t-test, t4 = 17.7, p = 0.0001, g = 2.8) trials than to the other two cued locations on Mismatch (M = 2.4, SD = 0.8) and Match (M = 1.7, SD = 0.8) trials.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: The number of fixations to the object was reduced on Mismatch relative to Match trials.
source: Notably, the number of fixations to the object was reduced on Mismatch relative to Match trials (paired t-test, t4 = −8.8, p = 0.0009, g = −0.6), indicating increased exploration during Mismatch.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: Fixation durations to objects were longer than matched spatial cues.
source: In addition, fixation durations to objects were longer than matched spatial cues (paired t-test, all t4 > 3.4, p < 0.03, g > 1.8) and were comparable between Match (M = 342 ms, SD = 88) and Mismatch trials (M = 388, SD = 131; paired t-test, t4 = 1.49, p = 0.21, g = 0.4).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: Prolonged viewing of the novel object-location (738 to 2188 ms after object presentation) was associated with memory updating.
source: Following initial visual orienting to the novel stimulus, prolonged viewing of the novel object-location (738 to 2188 ms after object presentation) was associated with memory updating (nonparametric cluster test, PFWE < 0.05, g = −0.7, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Viewing the original object-location during 998 to 1584 ms led to better memory for the original location.
source: Viewing the original object-location during this time period (from 998 to 1584 ms) led to better memory for the original location (nonparametric cluster test, PFWE < 0.05, g = 1.2, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Average power spectra from pre- and post-fixation intervals contained theta peaks irrespective of task condition and fixation target.
source: Average power spectra from pre- and post-fixation intervals contained theta peaks irrespective of task condition and fixation target (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: A majority of electrodes exhibited theta oscillations around the peak frequency both before (−750 to 50 ms) and after (−50 to 750 ms) fixation onsets to each ROI.
source: A majority of electrodes exhibited theta oscillations around this peak frequency both before (−750 to 50 ms) and after (−50 to 750 ms) fixation onsets to each ROI (see Table 2 for details).
evidence: This is a result from the experiment, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Significantly greater phase-locking around 5 Hz was observed prior to fixations to the original compared to the updated object-location on Mismatch trials.
source: We observed significantly greater phase-locking around 5 Hz prior to fixations to the original compared to the updated object-location on Mismatch trials (nonparametric cluster test, PFWE = 0.045, g = 1.2, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Significantly greater phase-locking was identified preceding fixations to the original object-location relative to fixations to objects presented in repeated locations (Match condition).
source: In an additional analysis, we also identified significantly greater phase-locking preceding fixations to the original object-location relative to fixations to objects presented in repeated locations (Match condition) during the same time-frequency window (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, PFWE = 0.04, g = 3.4, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Theta power was comparable before fixations to the original and updated object-locations.
source: Theta power was comparable before fixations to the original and updated object-locations (one sample t-test, t4 = −1.6, p = 0.17, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), indicating that differences in ITC did not result from reductions in theta magnitude.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: ITC measured during fixations to the updated location did not differ depending on the target of the next saccade.
source: First, ITC measured during fixations to the updated location did not differ depending on the target of the next saccade (i.e. either to the original or updated location; all PFWE > 0.15, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Significantly increased theta phase-locking was observed during the same time interval when fixations preceded by fixations to the updated object-location were excluded.
source: Second, we observed significantly increased theta phase-locking across subjects (one sample t-test, t4 = 2.95, p = 0.04) during the same time interval when we excluded fixations that were preceded by fixations to the updated object-location (which could cause stimulus-related processing to occur prior to the retrieval-guided fixation).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Significantly greater phase clustering followed fixations to updated compared to repeated object-locations.
source: Significantly (nonparametric cluster test, PFWE < 0.001, g = 1.2, n = 5 subjects) greater phase clustering followed fixations to updated compared to repeated object-locations (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 2d.

claim: ITC did not significantly differ between fixations to the Mismatch-original and Match-repeated locations.
source: This post-saccade phase-locking effect only followed fixations to updated locations, as ITC did not significantly differ between fixations to the Mismatch-original and Match-repeated locations.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: No significant differences were found between phase-locking following fixations to original and updated locations during Mismatch trials.
source: In addition, we did not find any significant differences between phase-locking following fixations to original and updated locations during Mismatch trials.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Significant differences (p < 0.05, uncorrected, permutation test) in phase between pre- and post-fixation time intervals were found in 27 out of 32 electrodes.
source: We found significant differences (p < 0.05, uncorrected, permutation test) in 27 out of 32 electrodes, significantly more than expected by chance (binomial test, p <0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Average theta phase preceding fixations to the original object-location occurred near the peak of theta (mean = 0.2 rad, 95% CI [−0.7 1.0]).
source: Average theta phase preceding fixations to the original object-location occurred near the peak of theta (mean = 0.2 rad, 95% CI [−0.7 1.0]).
evidence: This is a result from the experiment.

claim: Average theta phase following fixations to the updated object-location occurred near the trough of theta (mean = 2.8 rad, 95% CI [2.3 3.3]).
source: In contrast, the average theta phase following fixations to the updated object-location occurred near the trough of theta (mean = 2.8 rad, 95% CI [2.3 3.3]).
evidence: This is a result from the experiment.

claim: Permutation testing revealed consistent differences in phase across electrodes.
source: Permutation testing revealed consistent differences in phase across electrodes (ZF = 6.8, permutation p < 0.001, n = 32 electrodes).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: The distribution of phase in the interval preceding fixations to updated object-locations is indistinguishable from a uniform distribution.
source: First, the distribution of phase in the interval preceding fixations to updated object-locations is indistinguishable from a uniform distribution (Z = 1.04, p = 0.36, Rayleigh test, n = 32 electrodes).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Following fixations to the original object-location, phase was concentrated around theta troughs (mean = 2.9 rad, 95% CI [2.5 3.4]).
source: Second, following fixations to the original object-location, we found phase concentrated around theta troughs (mean = 2.9 rad, 95% CI [2.5 3.4]).
evidence: This is a result from the experiment.

claim: No significant subsequent memory effects were observed following fixations to the original object-location.
source: We observed no significant subsequent memory effects following fixations to the original object-location (Figure 4a, nonparametric cluster test, PFWE = 0.38, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: Greater ITC at frequencies ranging from 3 to 6 Hz following fixations to the updated location was associated with better memory for the original location on the final recognition test.
source: Greater ITC at frequencies ranging from 3 to 6 Hz following fixations to the updated location was associated with better memory for the original location on the final recognition test (nonparametric cluster test, PFWE < 0.0001, g = 0.5, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: The subsequent memory effect was significantly greater following fixations to updated as opposed to original object-locations.
source: The ability of hippocampal phase-locking to predict memory outcomes was specific to viewing updated object-locations; this subsequent memory effect was significantly greater following fixations to updated as opposed to original object-locations (Figure 4c, nonparametric cluster test, PFWE < 0.0001, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: Differences in subsequent memory effects could not be accounted for by differences in power.
source: Furthermore, these differences could not be accounted for by differences in power (all PFWE > 0.05, nonparametric cluster correction, n = 5 subjects).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Significantly increased ITC was observed preceding fixations to the original vs. updated locations on Mismatch trials after excluding fixations with extraneous saccades.
source: Notably, we observed significantly increased ITC preceding fixations to original vs. updated locations on Mismatch trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Similar increases in ITC were observed following fixations to updated vs. repeated objects after excluding fixations with extraneous saccades.
source: In addition, we observed similar increases in ITC following fixations to updated vs. repeated objects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), the magnitude of which predicted whether memory for the original object-location was maintained (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and 1c.

claim: Evidence for a reset of ongoing oscillations in the 8 to 13 Hz range was found following fixations to presented objects, irrespective of condition.
source: We found evidence for a reset of ongoing oscillations in the 8 to 13 Hz range following fixations to presented objects, irrespective of condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Significant differences in the magnitude of the phase reset effect were observed when comparing fixations to the original and updated object-location on Mismatch trials.
source: We observed significant differences (cluster PFWE = 0.006, t4 = −4.04, g = −1.14) in the magnitude of this phase reset effect when comparing fixations to the original and updated object-location on Mismatch trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Averaged ERPs locked to fixations to the original object-location exhibited increased power in the pre- vs. post-fixation interval at frequencies below 8 Hz.
source: Moreover, averaged ERPs locked to fixations to the original object-location exhibited increased power in the pre- vs. post-fixation interval at frequencies below 8 Hz (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, cluster PFWE = 0.004, t4 = −3.7, g = −1.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Phase resetting following fixations to the updated object-location on Mismatch trials marginally predicted memory for the original object-location.
source: Finally, phase resetting following fixations to the updated object-location on Mismatch trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c) marginally predicted memory for the original object-location (cluster PFWE = 0.09, t4 = 2.1, g = 1.08).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: No evidence for phase resets at frequencies above 13 Hz was observed.
source: We did not observe evidence for phase resets at frequencies above 13 Hz, near the upper border of the alpha band.
evidence: This is a result from the experiment.

claim: 25% of electrodes exhibited significant differences in PAC driven by associative novelty.
source: Across subjects, we found 25% of electrodes exhibited significant differences in PAC driven by associative novelty (i.e. differences between fixations to updated and repeated locations), significantly more than expected by chance (binomial test, p < 0.001, proportion difference = 0.2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Significantly greater PAC was found on 16% of electrodes compared to surrogate measures obtained by permuting theta phase across fixation events.
source: We found significantly greater PAC on 16% of electrodes (PFWE < 0.05, permutation test), compared to surrogate measures obtained by permuting theta phase across fixation events (significantly more than expected by chance, binomial test, p = 0.02).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Only 9% of electrodes exhibited significant differences in PAC preceding fixations to the original versus updated locations on Mismatch trials.
source: Only 9% of electrodes exhibited significant differences in PAC preceding fixations to the original versus updated locations on Mismatch trials (binomial test, p = 0.14, proportion difference = . 05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Significantly increased theta to gamma (80 to 100 Hz) PAC was found during fixations to updated object-locations.
source: We found significantly increased theta to gamma (80 to 100 Hz) PAC during fixations to updated object-locations (nonparametric cluster test, PFWE = 0.05, g = 1.2, n = 5 subjects), indicating that gamma amplitude was more dependent on theta phase when visual stimuli conflicted with memory (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: Increases in theta to high-gamma (130 to 150 Hz) PAC were significantly greater on trials where the original object-location was subsequently forgotten.
source: We found that increases in theta to high-gamma (130 to 150 Hz) PAC were significantly greater (nonparametric cluster test, PFWE = 0.04, g = −0.9, n = 5 subjects) on trials where the original object-location was subsequently forgotten (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 6b.

claim: No consistent relationship was observed between PAC and retrieval-related eye movements.
source: We did not observe a consistent relationship between PAC and retrieval-related eye movements, consistent with our electrode-level analyses.
evidence: This is a result from the experiment.

claim: Memory updating in the high-gamma range (130–150 Hz) produced greater subsequent memory effects compared to the 80 to 100 Hz gamma band associated with novelty detection.
source: This analysis suggested specificity of memory updating in the high-gamma range (130–150 Hz), as it produced greater subsequent memory effects compared to the 80 to 100 Hz gamma band associated with novelty detection (paired t-test, t4 = 2.6, p = 0.06, g = 0.7).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: No evidence for this level of specificity was observed associated with associative novelty.
source: On the other hand, we did not observe this level of specificity associated with associative novelty (paired t-test, t4 = −0.2, p = 0.84, g = −0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: No significant memory-related differences in PAC were observed in low-theta (1–3 Hz) and faster theta/alpha frequencies (7–10 Hz).
source: We did not observe significant memory-related differences in PAC in these ranges.
evidence: This is a result from the experiment.

claim: Significantly greater associative novelty-related changes in PAC were found when using 4–6 Hz phase compared to the faster theta/alpha band.
source: Directly comparing PAC effects across different ranges of theta, we found significantly greater associative novelty-related changes in PAC when using 4–6 Hz phase (identified via clear peaks in the power spectrum, see Figure 2b) to define the modulating frequency compared to the faster theta/alpha band (cluster PFWE = 0.01, t4 = 1.2, g = 0.7).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: Weak evidence for stronger effects than the low-theta band was found.
source: There was weak evidence for stronger effects than the low-theta band (cluster PFWE = 0.08, t4 = 1.9, g = 1.3), suggesting specificity of associative novelty-related PAC in the 4–6 Hz theta range.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: No evidence for frequency specificity was found when comparing updating-related PAC effects across different ranges of theta.
source: No evidence for frequency specificity was found when comparing updating-related PAC effects across different ranges of theta (all cluster PFWE > 0.13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: Theta waveform properties were significantly related to PAC in the 80-100 Hz frequency range for a minimal number of electrodes (range 2 to 5 electrodes).
source: We found that theta waveform properties were significantly related to PAC in this frequency range for a minimal number of electrodes (range 2 to 5 electrodes, see Table 4 for details), indicating that there was no consistent relation between theta waveform properties and novelty-related PAC.
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis, with reference to Table 4.

claim: Theta waveform properties did not influence theta to gamma (130–150 Hz) PAC associated with memory updating, with one notable exception.
source: Theta waveform properties did not influence theta to gamma (130–150 Hz) PAC associated with memory updating, with one notable exception (see Table 5 for details).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis, with reference to Table 5.

claim: Changes in theta power predicted trial-level differences in PAC in 22% of electrodes.
source: Changes in theta power predicted trial-level differences in PAC in 22% of electrodes, significantly more than expected by chance (p = 0.0008, binomial test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experiment.

claim: The same relation between PAC and detection of associative novelty and memory updating was found after regressing out variability explained by additional single-trial measures of theta amplitude, phase-locking, and waveform shape.
source: The results of this analysis revealed the same relation between PAC and detection of associative novelty and memory updating.
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis.

claim: Hippocampal recordings in humans have shown increased theta phase-locking and power following fixations to mismatched spatial locations.
source: Notably, we found increased theta phase-locking and power following fixations to mismatched spatial locations, consistent with previous hippocampal recordings in humans (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: fMRI work has established the involvement of the hippocampus in associative novelty detection and binding.
source: This extends previous fMRI work which has established the involvement of the hippocampus in associative novelty detection (Kumaran and Maguire, 2006; Kumaran and Maguire, 2007a) and binding (Bridge and Voss, 2014b), specifically supporting the idea that the hippocampus acts as a comparator between new sensory inputs and prior memory (Kumaran and Maguire, 2007b; Lisman, 1999; Lisman and Grace, 2005; Vinogradova, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many theories propose that theta cycles segregate neuronal activity into functional packets based on coactivation of neuronal populations during distinct time windows.
source: Many theories propose that theta cycles segregate neuronal activity into functional packets based on coactivation of neuronal populations during distinct time windows (Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Rennó-Costa and Tort, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Prior work has shown that increased theta to gamma PAC in hippocampus reflects successful encoding.
source: Prior work has shown that increased theta to gamma PAC in hippocampus reflects successful encoding (Lega et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Comparative studies between rodents and humans suggest that theta rhythms in the human are commonly observed at lower frequencies (e.g. 3 vs. 8 Hz) during exploratory behaviors.
source: Comparative studies between rodents and humans suggest that theta rhythms in the human are commonly observed at lower frequencies (e.g. 3 vs. 8 Hz) during exploratory behaviors (Watrous et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Studies have demonstrated multiple sources of theta rhythms in the medial temporal lobe, including a low-theta or delta band (1–4 Hz) in addition to the typical theta band (4–8 Hz).
source: Additionally, studies have demonstrated multiple sources of theta rhythms in the medial temporal lobe (Lega et al., 2012; Mormann et al., 2008), including a low-theta or delta band (1–4 Hz) in addition to the typical theta band (4–8 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Encoding-related increases in power and PAC are specific to the low-theta band.
source: Based on observations that encoding-related increases in power (Burke et al., 2013; Lega et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2018) and PAC (Lega et al., 2016) are specific to the low-theta band, it has been proposed that lower frequency theta in humans reflects a homologue of rodent theta (Jacobs, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher frequency theta effects have been observed during visual search.
source: Higher frequency theta effects have been observed during visual search (Hoffman et al., 2013), in which alignment between saccades and theta oscillations was focused between 6–8 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Saccades during visual exploration caused resets in hippocampal oscillations predominantly in the 8–11 Hz range in nonhuman primates.
source: Our findings that fixations to objects caused theta phase resets in the 6–12 Hz range are consistent with work in nonhuman primates (Jutras et al., 2013), which demonstrated that saccades during visual exploration caused resets in hippocampal oscillations predominantly in the 8–11 Hz range.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Theories of hippocampal organization emphasize functional segregation along its long axis.
source: Drawn primarily from animal models, theories of hippocampal organization emphasize functional segregation along its long axis (Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Strange et al., 2014), with general agreement regarding a role of the anterior (ventral in rodents) hippocampus in emotion and affect, and the posterior (dorsal in rodents) hippocampus in spatial navigation and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent theories emphasize gradients in the scale of representations along the hippocampal long axis.
source: Our findings are consistent with recent theories that emphasize gradients in the scale of representations along the hippocampal long axis (Bellmund et al., 2018; Poppenk et al., 2013) with transitions from general to precise representations in the anterior to posterior direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Modulation of hippocampal theta by eye movements has been observed in the anterior hippocampus of non-human primates.
source: However, modulation of hippocampal theta by eye movements has also been observed in the anterior hippocampus of non-human primates (Jutras et al., 2013), suggesting a conserved mechanism across primates.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cells within the entorhinal cortex of macaques code the location of fixations in a grid-like fashion during free viewing.
source: Cells within the entorhinal cortex of macaques code the location of fixations in a grid-like fashion during free viewing (Killian et al., 2012), serving as a potential mechanism to provide a scale-invariant representation of fixation locations within the scene (Bicanski and Burgess, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Similar grid-like modulation of entorhinal activity has been observed in humans using fMRI.
source: Similar grid-like modulation of entorhinal activity has been observed in humans using fMRI (Julian et al., 2018; Nau et al., 2018), providing converging evidence across species that the entorhinal system may provide a spatial framework for memory-guided viewing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Free-viewing paradigms with hippocampal damage show disruptions in viewing behaviors.
source: Causal manipulation of hippocampal theta, including stimulation-based approaches could be used to test this hypothesis, which is supported by growing evidence for disruptions in viewing behaviors from amnesic patients with hippocampal damage (Hannula et al., 2007; Lucas et al., 2019; Olsen et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2000; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Five subjects with refractory epilepsy performed the associative memory task.
source: Five subjects (three male; see Table 6 for demographic information) with refractory epilepsy performed our associative memory task during their stay at Northwestern Memorial Hospital (Chicago, IL).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All subjects had depth electrodes implanted in the hippocampus as part of neurosurgical monitoring prior to elective surgery.
source: All subjects had depth electrodes implanted in the hippocampus as part of neurosurgical monitoring prior to elective surgery.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Written informed consent was acquired from all subjects prior to participation in the research protocol in accordance with the Northwestern University Institutional Review Board.
source: Written informed consent was acquired from all subjects prior to participation in the research protocol in accordance with the Northwestern University Institutional Review Board.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: Objects were 128 trial-unique images of real-life objects from the Bank of Standardized Stimuli.
source: Objects were 128 trial-unique images of real-life objects from the Bank of Standardized Stimuli (Brodeur et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli, with a citation.

claim: Eye movements were recorded at 500 Hz using an Eyelink 1000 remote tracking system.
source: Eye movements were recorded at 500 Hz using an Eyelink 1000 remote tracking system (SR Research, Ontario, Canada).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Electrophysiological data were recorded to a clinical reference using a Nihon Kohden amplifier with a sample rate of 1–2 kHz with a bandpass filter from 0.6 to 600 Hz.
source: Electrophysiological data were recorded to a clinical reference using a Nihon Kohden amplifier with a sample rate of 1–2 kHz with a bandpass filter from 0.6 to 600 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Data were re-referenced to a bipolar montage and downsampled to 500 Hz as part of preprocessing.
source: Data were re-referenced to a bipolar montage and downsampled to 500 Hz as part of preprocessing.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methods.

claim: Electrodes that exhibited inter-ictal spiking were excluded from analysis.
source: To rule out the possibility that epileptiform activity influenced our analyses, electrodes that exhibited inter-ictal spiking were excluded from analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methods.

claim: All analyses were repeated after excluding contacts within the seizure onset zone (two electrodes in S3).
source: In addition, all analyses were repeated after excluding contacts within the seizure onset zone (two electrodes in S3).
evidence: This is a description of a control analysis.

claim: The observed results were qualitatively identical, with no statistical differences when including all electrodes.
source: The observed results were qualitatively identical, with no statistical differences when including all electrodes (all p > 0.05).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis.

claim: Post-implant CT (n = 4) or T1 weighted structural images (n = 1) were coregistered with presurgical T1 weighted structural MRIs using SPM12.
source: Post-implant CT (n = 4) or T1 weighted structural images (n = 1) were coregistered with presurgical T1 weighted structural MRIs using SPM12.
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical localization methods.

claim: Subdural electrodes were localized by reconstructing whole-brain cortical surfaces from pre-implant T1-weighted MRIs using the computational anatomy toolbox and snapping electrode centroids to the cortical surface based on energy minimization.
source: Subdural electrodes were localized by reconstructing whole-brain cortical surfaces from pre-implant T1-weighted MRIs using the computational anatomy toolbox (Dahnke et al., 2013) and snapping electrode centroids to the cortical surface based on energy minimization (Dykstra et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical localization methods, with citations.

claim: Bipolar recordings were decomposed into measures of spectral phase and power using the continuous Morlet wavelet transform (wave number 5) across 30 logarithmically spaced frequencies from 1 to 10 Hz.
source: To examine oscillatory processes in the hippocampus, we decomposed bipolar recordings into measures of spectral phase and power using the continuous Morlet wavelet transform (wave number 5) across 30 logarithmically spaced frequencies from 1 to 10 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the spectral decomposition methods.

claim: The presence of oscillatory components was evaluated by testing the equality of variances between aperiodic and full models.
source: The presence of oscillatory components was then evaluated by testing the equality of variances between aperiodic and full models.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis methods.

claim: A nonparametric permutation-based approach was adopted to correct for multiple comparisons across time and frequencies.
source: We adopted a nonparametric permutation-based approach (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007) to correct for multiple comparisons across time and frequencies.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods, with a citation.

claim: The sample size was determined based on prior work in humans and nonhuman primates, which reported robust modulations in hippocampal theta due to visual sampling with sample sizes ranging from two to six subjects.
source: Our sample size was determined based on prior work in humans and nonhuman primates (Hoffman et al., 2013; Jutras et al., 2013; Staudigl et al., 2017), which reported robust modulations in hippocampal theta due to visual sampling with a sample sizes ranging from two to six subjects.
evidence: This is a justification for the sample size, with citations.

claim: Significant retrieval effects were observed in about one third of all electrodes.
source: We observed significant retrieval effects in about one third of all electrodes, and more than half showed significant novelty and subsequent memory effects.
evidence: This is a summary of electrode-level results.

claim: More than half of electrodes showed significant novelty and subsequent memory effects.
source: We observed significant retrieval effects in about one third of all electrodes, and more than half showed significant novelty and subsequent memory effects.
evidence: This is a summary of electrode-level results.

claim: The hippocampus coordinates memory-guided eye movements.
source: Phase-locking at the peak of theta preceded fixations to retrieved locations, indicating that the hippocampus coordinates memory-guided eye movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling predicted memory updating.
source: Theta-gamma phase amplitude coupling increased during fixations to conflicting visual content, but predicted memory updating.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiment.

claim: Interactions between encoding and retrieval support memory updating.
source: Interactions between encoding and retrieval support many important functions, including memory updating, which requires comparing novel sensory inputs to prior memories and integrating new content into memory representations (Bridge and Paller, 2012; Bridge and Voss, 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The underlying novelty and retrieval processes have not been segregated as they unfold during learning.
source: However, the underlying novelty and retrieval processes have not been segregated as they unfold, in part because it is difficult to segregate these mechanisms in real time, as they interact continuously during learning.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in prior research.

claim: Eye movements provide an ideal behavioral measure to dissect learning processes on a moment-to-moment basis.
source: Thus, eye movements provide an ideal behavioral measure to dissect learning processes on a moment-to-moment basis.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of eye movements as a measure.

claim: The interaction of fast gamma and theta oscillations in the hippocampus could play a key role in coordinating interactions between encoding and retrieval during exploration.
source: The interaction of fast gamma and theta oscillations in the hippocampus could play a key role in coordinating interactions between encoding and retrieval during exploration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior knowledge.

claim: Fast and slow gamma separately mediate encoding of novel information and memory retrieval.
source: Recent work has also identified unique theta-nested gamma oscillations observed within individual theta cycles (Lopes-Dos-Santos et al., 2018), providing support for the notion that fast and slow gamma separately mediate encoding of novel information and memory retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It is not known how changes in PAC during exploration translate from animal models to similar behaviors in humans.
source: Because evidence for memory-related hippocampal theta to gamma PAC in humans has primarily focused on verbal learning tasks (Lega et al., 2016; Mormann et al., 2005), it is not known how changes in PAC during exploration translate from animal models to similar behaviors in humans.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: Theta oscillations would influence when eye movements were driven by either associative novelty or memory retrieval, through theta-dependent modulation of neuronal firing.
source: We hypothesized that theta oscillations would influence when eye movements were driven by either associative novelty or memory retrieval, through theta-dependent modulation of neuronal firing.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: If the strength of encoding and retrieval are modulated by theta phase, fixations driven by each process should be phase-locked to the theta rhythm.
source: If the strength of encoding and retrieval are modulated by theta phase, fixations driven by each process should be phase-locked to the theta rhythm.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: Eye-movements tied to distinct encoding and retrieval processes should occur at distinct phases of theta with variation in hippocampal PAC.
source: In addition, eye-movements tied to distinct encoding and retrieval processes should occur at distinct phases of theta with variation in hippocampal PAC.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: Interplay between memory processes and visual sampling during Mismatch trials determined whether memory updating would occur.
source: These findings suggest that interplay between memory processes and visual sampling during Mismatch trials determined whether memory updating would occur.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Hippocampal signaling prior to fixations would reflect a memory-guided initiation of the upcoming eye movement.
source: We reasoned that hippocampal signaling prior to fixations would reflect a memory-guided initiation of the upcoming eye movement, whereas signaling following fixations would reflect a memory-based reaction to visual input.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the interpretation of the data.

claim: Hippocampal signaling following fixations would reflect a memory-based reaction to visual input.
source: We reasoned that hippocampal signaling prior to fixations would reflect a memory-guided initiation of the upcoming eye movement, whereas signaling following fixations would reflect a memory-based reaction to visual input.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the interpretation of the data.

claim: The observed pre-fixation theta effects reflect a retrieval mechanism, rather than novelty-related processes that initiate memory retrieval.
source: These findings suggest that the observed pre-fixation theta effects reflect a retrieval mechanism, rather than novelty-related processes that initiate memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Modulation of theta phase by two processes: retrieval processing preceding fixations to the original location and novelty processing following fixations to the updated location.
source: Taken together, our comparison of ITC between fixation targets suggests modulation of theta phase by two processes: retrieval processing preceding fixations to the original location and novelty processing following fixations to the updated location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: If theta phase-locking preceding fixations to original object-locations was driven by theta-dependent retrieval mechanisms, preferred phase angles would be near the peak of the theta.
source: If theta phase-locking preceding fixations to original object-locations was driven by theta-dependent retrieval mechanisms, we would predict preferred phase angles near the peak of the theta.
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical models.

claim: Phase-locking would begin at the trough of theta oscillations during fixations to updated object-locations, as theta troughs are associated with increased sensory inputs from the entorhinal cortex that support encoding of the environment.
source: On the other hand, we would predict the phase-locking to begin at the trough of theta oscillations during fixations to updated object-locations, as theta troughs are associated with increased sensory inputs from the entorhinal cortex that support encoding of the environment.
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical models.

claim: The timing of memory-dependent fixations depend upon the phase of theta.
source: These results provide additional evidence that the timing of memory-dependent fixations depend upon the phase of theta.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: If the observed phase-locking of eye movements to hippocampal theta reflects encoding and retrieval operations, the strength of coherence between visual sampling and theta would determine memory performance.
source: If the observed phase-locking of eye movements to hippocampal theta reflects encoding and retrieval operations, we would predict that the strength of coherence between visual sampling and theta determines memory performance.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: The reset of hippocampal theta by novel sensory information may be a major determinant of memory performance on this task.
source: These results suggest that the reset of hippocampal theta by novel sensory information may be a major determinant of memory performance on this task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The pattern of viewing behavior on Mismatch trials indicates that the detection of the updated object-location precedes retrieval-guided viewing of the original object-location.
source: Moreover, the pattern of viewing behavior on Mismatch trials indicates that the detection of the updated object-location precedes retrieval-guided viewing of the original object-location (Figure 1d), suggesting that retrieval-related changes in ITC were predictive of memory-guided visual exploration but not memory outcomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, with reference to Figure 1d.

claim: Retrieval-related changes in ITC were predictive of memory-guided visual exploration but not memory outcomes.
source: Moreover, the pattern of viewing behavior on Mismatch trials indicates that the detection of the updated object-location precedes retrieval-guided viewing of the original object-location (Figure 1d), suggesting that retrieval-related changes in ITC were predictive of memory-guided visual exploration but not memory outcomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, with reference to Figure 1d.

claim: The observed effects were truly related to the fixations of interest, rather than preceding or following eye movements.
source: These results indicate that the observed phase effects are likely related to fixations of interest, rather than sequential behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control analysis findings.

claim: The observed interactions between theta phase and gamma amplitude likely reflect distinct processing states in hippocampal networks, wherein asynchronous local activity is necessary to segregate novel perceptual information from previously encoded memories.
source: The observed interactions between theta phase and gamma amplitude likely reflect distinct processing states in hippocampal networks, wherein asynchronous local activity is necessary to segregate novel perceptual information from previously encoded memories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Observed differences in PAC resulted from nested oscillations, as opposed to amplitude modulation of sharp waveforms or other changes to the theta waveform.
source: Evaluation of theta waveform properties revealed that memory-related differences in PAC resulted from nested oscillations, as opposed to amplitude modulation of sharp waveforms or other changes to the theta waveform.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control analysis findings.

claim: Distinct neurophysiological states, defined by theta phase and modulation of gamma amplitude, indicated when viewing was driven by memory as opposed to novel information in the environment.
source: Distinct neurophysiological states, defined by theta phase and modulation of gamma amplitude, indicated when viewing was driven by memory as opposed to novel information in the environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Translating findings from rodents to observations in humans regarding theta rhythms has proven challenging.
source: Despite the emerging consensus in the rodent that theta oscillations in the hippocampus are responsible for segregating neuronal computations involved in encoding and retrieval operations (Colgin, 2015; Colgin, 2016; Hasselmo et al., 2002), translating these findings to observations in humans has proven challenging.
evidence: This is a statement about challenges in the field, with citations.

claim: The difference in theta frequency between rodents and humans stems from the emphasis on visual information in the task, resulting in a task-dependence in the frequency of theta oscillations.
source: We believe this difference stems from the emphasis on visual information in our task, resulting in a task-dependence in the frequency of theta oscillations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Multiple factors could account for changes in the speed of hippocampal theta, including the type of representation being processed in the medial temporal lobe, spatial attention required by a given task, or the rate of fixations.
source: Multiple factors could account for changes in the speed of hippocampal theta, including the type of representation being processed in the medial temporal lobe (Watrous et al., 2013b), spatial attention required by a given task, or the rate of fixations.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors that could influence theta frequency, with a citation.

claim: Future studies are necessary to determine what factors determine the speed of hippocampal theta oscillations and their relevance to different forms of memory.
source: Future studies are necessary to determine what factors determine the speed of hippocampal theta oscillations and their relevance to different forms of memory.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The findings are consistent with recent theories that emphasize gradients in the scale of representations along the hippocampal long axis with transitions from general to precise representations in the anterior to posterior direction.
source: Our findings are consistent with recent theories that emphasize gradients in the scale of representations along the hippocampal long axis (Bellmund et al., 2018; Poppenk et al., 2013) with transitions from general to precise representations in the anterior to posterior direction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theories, with citations.

claim: The emphasis of global spatial relations in the task may account for the observed effects within anterior hippocampus.
source: Thus, the emphasis of global spatial relations in our task (i.e. the relative positions of the original and updated locations rather than precise locations) may account for the observed effects within anterior hippocampus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Memory-guided exploratory behaviors depend upon interactions between distributed cortical systems.
source: While our analysis of theta oscillations was restricted to electrodes in the hippocampus (or adjacent white matter), memory-guided exploratory behaviors depend upon interactions between distributed cortical systems (Voss et al., 2017), particularly those involved in representing features within a scene, the spatial relations between these features, and transforming these memory representations into an oculomotor plan based on current visual input.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader context of the findings, with a citation.

claim: Synchronous theta oscillations between the hippocampus and entorhinal systems would provide the spatial coding necessary to inform the oculomotor system of memory-relevant information.
source: As such, synchronous theta oscillations between the hippocampus and entorhinal systems would provide the spatial coding necessary to inform the oculomotor system of memory-relevant information.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms underlying the findings.

claim: Examining entorhinal-hippocampal synchrony and interactions between the hippocampus and other cortical systems should be a key aim for future studies.
source: Although we were limited by electrode coverage, examining entorhinal-hippocampal synchrony and interactions between the hippocampus and other cortical systems should be a key aim for future studies.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: It is unclear how stereotyped retrieval-dependent eye movements would be during unconstrained visual exploration.
source: Thus, it is unclear how stereotyped these retrieval-dependent eye movements would be during unconstrained visual exploration.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: Free-viewing paradigms could build on this theoretical framework and determine the extent to which hippocampal-dependent viewing behaviors occur without task constraints.
source: Free-viewing paradigms could build on this theoretical framework and determine the extent to which hippocampal-dependent viewing behaviors occur without task constraints.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: It is likely that the hippocampus plays a causal role in generating retrieval-dependent eye movements.
source: Given the observed retrieval phase-locking effects occurred well before saccade initiation, it is likely that the hippocampus plays a causal role in generating these eye movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Causal manipulation of hippocampal theta, including stimulation-based approaches could be used to test the hypothesis that the hippocampus plays a causal role in generating retrieval-dependent eye movements.
source: Causal manipulation of hippocampal theta, including stimulation-based approaches could be used to test this hypothesis, which is supported by growing evidence for disruptions in viewing behaviors from amnesic patients with hippocampal damage (Hannula et al., 2007; Lucas et al., 2019; Olsen et al., 2016; Ryan et al., 2000; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions, with citations.

claim: Hippocampal theta could coordinate visual sampling between novel content in the environment and memory-rich spatial locations.
source: Akin to spatial attention shifting between multiple locations relevant to a task at hand (Landau et al., 2015; Re et al., 2019), hippocampal theta could coordinate visual sampling between novel content in the environment and memory-rich spatial locations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research, with citations.

claim: The hippocampus contributes to memory-guided behaviors through coordinated sampling of current and past perceptual states.
source: The hippocampus thereby contributes to memory-guided behaviors through coordinated sampling of current and past perceptual states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: If hippocampal PAC supports encoding, increased PAC could strengthen associations between objects and updated locations.
source: If hippocampal PAC supports encoding, increased PAC could strengthen associations between objects and updated locations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying memory updating.

claim: During the final memory test, the strength of associations between objects and updated locations interferes with memory for the original location, resulting in forgetting.
source: During the final memory test, the strength of these associations interferes with memory for the original location, resulting in forgetting.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying memory updating.

claim: Multiple processes could contribute to memory updating, including weakening of older memories during new learning or biased competition between memories at retrieval.
source: Despite this account, we cannot rule out the possibility that multiple processes contribute to memory updating. For example, updating could result from weakening of older memories during new learning or biased competition between memories at retrieval (Kuhl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about alternative explanations, with a citation.

claim: The experimental design cannot distinguish between different accounts of memory updating.
source: Although our experimental design cannot distinguish between these accounts (i.e. memory updating necessarily causes forgetting of the original object-location), our findings clearly demonstrate that increased PAC predicts the formation of novel memories at the expense of prior learning.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: Increased PAC predicts the formation of novel memories at the expense of prior learning.
source: Although our experimental design cannot distinguish between these accounts (i.e. memory updating necessarily causes forgetting of the original object-location), our findings clearly demonstrate that increased PAC predicts the formation of novel memories at the expense of prior learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The lack of theta-dependent modulation of gamma amplitude during retrieval could result from biased sampling to the anterior hippocampus and potential obscuring of narrowband gamma signals due to summation across larger neuronal populations.
source: While we did not observe theta-dependent modulation of gamma amplitude during retrieval, this could result from a number of methodological constrains, such as biased sampling to the anterior hippocampus and potential obscuring of narrowband gamma signals commonly observed in microelectrodes due to summation across larger neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for a null finding.

claim: The consistent timing of theta phase-locking and power effects following fixation onset provide evidence that hippocampal theta is involved in the computation of mismatch signals.
source: The consistent timing of these effects following fixation onset provide further evidence that hippocampal theta is involved in the computation of mismatch signals, as opposed to providing signals of perceptual familiarity that could guide viewing to novel locations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Hippocampal theta is not involved in providing signals of perceptual familiarity that could guide viewing to novel locations.
source: The consistent timing of these effects following fixation onset provide further evidence that hippocampal theta is involved in the computation of mismatch signals, as opposed to providing signals of perceptual familiarity that could guide viewing to novel locations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The hippocampus acts as a comparator between new sensory inputs and prior memory.
source: This extends previous fMRI work which has established the involvement of the hippocampus in associative novelty detection (Kumaran and Maguire, 2006; Kumaran and Maguire, 2007a) and binding (Bridge and Voss, 2014b), specifically supporting the idea that the hippocampus acts as a comparator between new sensory inputs and prior memory (Kumaran and Maguire, 2007b; Lisman, 1999; Lisman and Grace, 2005; Vinogradova, 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theories, with citations.

claim: Theta oscillations organize high-frequency computations across hippocampal networks.
source: In addition, theta to high-gamma PAC increased during the detection of novel spatial information, consistent with theta oscillations organizing high-frequency computations across hippocampal networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The models of theta-dependent segregation of encoding and retrieval explain when memory-driven eye movements occur in humans, particularly when there are demands for memory encoding and retrieval to co-occur.
source: In doing so, we show these models explain when memory-driven eye movements occur in humans, particularly when there are demands for memory encoding and retrieval to co-occur.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Hippocampal involvement in visual exploration is supported by the data.
source: These data support theories of active hippocampal involvement in visual exploration (Voss et al., 2017) and provide novel evidence that theta oscillations support both retrieval- and novelty-dependent viewing behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, with a citation.

claim: Theta oscillations support both retrieval- and novelty-dependent viewing behaviors.
source: These data support theories of active hippocampal involvement in visual exploration (Voss et al., 2017) and provide novel evidence that theta oscillations support both retrieval- and novelty-dependent viewing behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, with a citation.

claim: Hippocampal memory representations are used to guide saccades to behaviorally relevant locations.
source: Based upon electrophysiological studies in humans and primates (Hoffman et al., 2013; Jutras et al., 2013), it has become apparent that hippocampal memory representations are used to guide saccades to behaviorally relevant locations (Meister and Buffalo, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual exploration of novel, but not repeated, scenes leads to a reset of hippocampal theta oscillations.
source: Of particular relevance to the present work, visual exploration of novel, but not repeated, scenes leads to a reset of hippocampal theta oscillations (Jutras et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The consistency of the hippocampal phase reset predicts the success of novel encoding.
source: The consistency of this hippocampal phase reset predicts the success of novel encoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research.

claim: Evidence for conserved hippocampal processing in humans is provided by demonstrating increased phase consistency of theta oscillations following fixations to novel locations, which were associated with improved memory performance.
source: In the present work, we provide evidence for conserved hippocampal processing in humans, by demonstrating increased phase consistency of theta oscillations following fixations to novel locations, which were further associated with improved memory performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Visual exploration of scenes is associated with hippocampal function, as the number of fixations during encoding predicted both hippocampal activity and subsequent memory.
source: Recent work using fMRI (Liu et al., 2017) also suggests that visual exploration of scenes is associated with hippocampal function, as the number of fixations during encoding predicted both hippocampal activity and subsequent memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The relationship between hippocampal activity and viewing behavior was limited to novel (but not repeated) stimuli.
source: This relationship between hippocampal activity and viewing behavior was limited to novel (but not repeated) stimuli, suggesting hippocampal activity and exploratory eye movements are linked specifically when encoding novel content.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior research.

claim: Previous studies have tied hippocampal activity to retrieval-guided eye movements.
source: Taken together with previous studies that have tied hippocampal activity to retrieval-guided eye movements (Bridge et al., 2017; Hannula and Ranganath, 2009) these results provide evidence that visual exploration is dependent upon the interplay of separate retrieval and novelty-detection mechanisms that underpin learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual exploration is dependent upon the interplay of separate retrieval and novelty-detection mechanisms that underpin learning.
source: Taken together with previous studies that have tied hippocampal activity to retrieval-guided eye movements (Bridge et al., 2017; Hannula and Ranganath, 2009) these results provide evidence that visual exploration is dependent upon the interplay of separate retrieval and novelty-detection mechanisms that underpin learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and prior research, with citations.
